concepts.name: Socialisation and the family
concepts.description: Form 1. Meaning of socialisation (learning the norms, values, skills and roles of society), primary and secondary socialisation in outline, the agents of socialisation listed, and the home as the first agent: the role of each family member (mother, father, grandparents, aunts (vatete/ubabakazi), uncles (sekuru/umalume), older siblings) in teaching language, manners, work, values and identity. The school, peers, community, religion and media as agents are separate concepts.

concepts.name: The school and peers in socialisation
concepts.description: Form 2. How the school socialises learners (school rules, punctuality, discipline, uniform, routines, teamwork, sport and clubs, teachers as role models, the National Schools Pledge mentioned only as an example); the role of peers (friendship, interaction, cliques, role models), positive and negative peer pressure, and how to choose and resist influence responsibly.

concepts.name: The community and religious beliefs in socialisation
concepts.description: Form 3. How the community socialises young people (elders, neighbours, community gatherings and work parties, rituals and ceremonies, traditional leaders, sanctions and praise) and the role of religious beliefs in socialisation: indigenous religion, Christianity, Islam and other faiths in Zimbabwe, presented respectfully and without ranking faiths (teachings on conduct, worship, rites, religious groups and youth organisations). Details of indigenous religious practices are her.identity.religious-practices.

concepts.name: The media in socialisation and its responsible use
concepts.description: Forms 2 and 3. Types of media (print: newspapers, magazines, books; electronic: radio, television, film; social media), the role and effects of the media in socialisation (information, education, entertainment, role models, values, advertising, stereotypes), advantages and disadvantages of the media as a socialising agent, appropriate and inappropriate content, and the responsible use of media (checking sources, recognising false information, age-appropriate content). Devices, the internet and online behaviour as ICT are her.socialisation.ict.

concepts.name: Information and Communication Technologies in socialisation
concepts.description: Form 4. The role of ICT (mobile phones, computers, the internet, social networking, messaging, online learning) in socialisation, its positive effects (access to information, communication with family, learning, enterprise) and negative effects (cyberbullying, addiction, exposure to harmful content, loss of indigenous values, privacy and online safety risks, digital footprint), and responsible, safe use. General mass-media effects are her.socialisation.media.

concepts.name: Types of families and the roles of family members
concepts.description: Form 1. Types of families (nuclear, extended, one-parent, child-headed, monogamous and polygamous families), relationships within each type, and the roles of family members in the home, the community and the nation. The advantages and disadvantages of monogamous and polygamous marriage are her.identity.marriage-types.

concepts.name: Language and national identity
concepts.description: Form 1. How language expresses and promotes identity (names, greetings, songs, oral traditions, ways of thinking), the link between language and personal, community and national identity, and the role of language in unity and in passing on heritage. The kinds of wise sayings (proverbs, idioms, riddles, folklore) are her.identity.wise-sayings; the languages and cultures of Zimbabwe's peoples are her.identity.languages-cultures.

concepts.name: Indigenous languages and cultures of the people of Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 2. The peoples, languages and cultures of Zimbabwe (Shona, Ndebele, Venda, Kalanga, Tonga, Shangani/Tsonga, Nambya, Ndau, Sotho, Tswana, Chewa, Chibarwe, Xhosa, Koisan and others), the 16 officially recognised languages of the Constitution (section 6), including sign language, cultural features such as dress, food, music and crafts in outline, and the importance of upholding indigenous languages and cultures. Respectful and equal treatment of every group.

concepts.name: Indigenous wise sayings: proverbs, idioms, riddles and folklore
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 4. Types of indigenous wise sayings (proverbs (tsumo/izaga), idioms (madimikira/izisho), riddles (zvirahwe/iziphicaphicwano), folk tales (ngano/inganekwane)), their features and examples with meanings, and their significance (teaching values, advice, entertainment, identity, sharpening thinking). Forms of entertainment such as games and dance are her.culture.entertainment.

concepts.name: Indigenous hunting and production tools
concepts.description: Form 1. Indigenous hunting tools (traps, snares, spears, bows and arrows, clubs, hunting dogs as a practice) and production tools (hoes, axes, grinding stones, mortar and pestle (duri and mutswi), baskets, winnowing baskets, clay pots, bellows for iron working), how each was made and used, and their importance for identity and heritage today. Iron-Age technology in history is her.precolonial.early-iron-age.

concepts.name: Personal identity and national identification documents
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Forms of personal identity (name, family, totem, language, religion, nationality, documents), the national identification documents (birth certificate, national identity card, passport), the main contents of each, how they are obtained from the Registrar General in outline, and their importance (proof of citizenship, access to education, employment, voting, travel). Citizenship law is her.constitution.citizenship; totems are her.identity.totems.

concepts.name: Totems, totem praises and genealogy
concepts.description: Form 2. Meaning of totem (mutupo/isibongo) and sub-totem, examples of common totems (e.g. Shumba, Moyo, Dube, Ncube, Soko, Gumbo, Nyathi) and totem praises (detembo/izibongo) in outline, tracing genealogy and drawing a family tree, and the purposes of the totem system (identity, preventing marriage between close relatives, conservation of the totem animal, unity, respect, social order).

concepts.name: Indigenous herbs and their uses
concepts.description: Form 2. Examples of plants used in indigenous health practices (e.g. aloe, blackjack, and others named in the syllabus), the traditional uses people make of them, how indigenous knowledge of herbs is passed on, its value as heritage and the need to conserve these plants. Safety: no claims that herbs cure diseases; stress dosage risks, the need to consult trained health workers, and regulation of traditional medicine in outline.

concepts.name: Family, community and indigenous gatherings in shaping identity
concepts.description: Form 3. The role of the family and the community in shaping one's identity, and indigenous community gatherings, ceremonies and events (rain-making ceremonies (mukwerera/ukucela izulu), work parties (nhimbe/ilima), funerals, the bringing-home ceremony (kurova guva/umbuyiso), harvest and thanksgiving gatherings), their purpose, the ceremonial tools used, and how they build belonging. Birth and death rites as rites are her.culture.birth-death-rites.

concepts.name: Types of marriage: indigenous and contemporary
concepts.description: Form 4. Indigenous marriages (monogamous and polygamous) with their advantages and disadvantages presented fairly; contemporary marriages (civil and customary marriages, religious marriages) with their features, advantages and disadvantages; the legal minimum marriage age of 18; the 2022 marriage law reform in outline only if certain. Marriage procedures such as lobola are her.culture.marriage-practices; roles of spouses are her.culture.men-women-marriage.

concepts.name: Indigenous religious practices
concepts.description: Form 4. Indigenous belief in God (Mwari/uMlimo/Nyadenga), ancestral spirits (midzimu/amadlozi), territorial (mhondoro) spirits and the role of spirit mediums, forms of spirits as described in the syllabus, religious practices and rituals (bira, rain-making, kurova guva/umbuyiso, sacred places such as Njelele), the significance of these practices, and relations with other faiths, all presented respectfully and descriptively.

concepts.name: The concept of Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu
concepts.description: Form 1. Meaning of Unhu/Ubuntu/Vumunhu (being human through others), its attributes (tolerance, integrity, oneness, respect, humility, honesty, compassion, hospitality, sharing), examples of behaviour that shows or lacks Unhu, and its importance for individuals, families, communities and the nation. Norms and values in specific settings are her.culture.norms-values and her.culture.workplace.

concepts.name: Norms and values at home, school and in the community
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Meaning of norms and values and the difference between them, norms and values peculiar to the home, the school and the community (respect, courtesy, discipline, honesty, hard work, cooperation), how they are taught and enforced (praise, sanctions), and their importance. The workplace is her.culture.workplace; foreign influences are her.culture.foreign-influences.

concepts.name: Norms and values at the workplace
concepts.description: Form 3. Workplace norms and values (punctuality, responsibility, accountability, integrity, respect, confidentiality, teamwork, dress codes, safety), why they matter, and threats to them (corruption, absenteeism, theft, harassment, poor work ethic) with ways of upholding them.

concepts.name: Main features of indigenous Zimbabwean culture
concepts.description: Form 2. The main features of indigenous culture (language, family and kinship, totems, religion and beliefs, food, dress, music, dance and crafts, social organisation and leadership, values such as respect for elders and communal sharing), and why norms and values in indigenous culture matter. Details of each feature are taught in their own concepts.

concepts.name: Zimbabwean and foreign norms and values; threats to indigenous culture
concepts.description: Form 4. Comparison of Zimbabwean and foreign norms and values (dress, greetings, family roles, individualism and communalism), their significance, and threats to indigenous culture (foreign influence, media and the internet, urbanisation, migration, globalisation, some religious attitudes, loss of language), with ways of preserving culture (teaching languages, festivals, museums, family practice). Balanced: foreign influence is not all negative.

concepts.name: Inheritance and heirship in indigenous families
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Meaning of inheritance and heirship, tangible inheritance (property, livestock) and intangible inheritance (name, language, norms, values, office), indigenous inheritance and heirship practices (choice of heir, the role of the extended family, sharing of the estate (kugova nhaka), the heir's duties), their importance and their weaknesses. Wills and contemporary law are her.culture.inheritance-contemporary.

concepts.name: Inheritance and heirship in contemporary families
concepts.description: Form 3. Inheritance in contemporary families and societies: the concept of a will and why it matters, inheriting without a will (spouses and children as beneficiaries in outline), the role of the Master of the High Court in outline, property-grabbing and its effects, and a comparison of indigenous and contemporary practices. Exact percentages and legal detail only if certain.

concepts.name: Rites of passage and the age of consent
concepts.description: Form 1. Meaning of rites of passage, rites associated with adolescence in different ethnic groups in Zimbabwe described respectfully and without graphic detail, their significance and implications, and the law on the age of consent to sex and to marriage (18 for marriage under the Constitution) with why these protect children. Birth and death rites are her.culture.birth-death-rites.

concepts.name: Indigenous and contemporary courtship practices
concepts.description: Forms 1, 2 and 3. Indigenous courtship practices of different ethnic groups (the role of intermediaries, meeting places, tokens of love, involvement of aunts and uncles), contemporary courtship practices (social, religious, western-influenced, online), their advantages and disadvantages, and a comparison and evaluation of the two. Marriage procedures are her.culture.marriage-practices.

concepts.name: Indigenous marriage practices and marriage counselling
concepts.description: Forms 2 and 3. Indigenous marriage practices (the go-between (munyai/umkhongi), bride wealth (roora/lobola), handing over the bride (kuperekwa/umthimba), the roles of aunts (vatete/ubabakazi) and uncles (sekuru/umalume) as marriage counsellors and the counselling process), forms of indigenous marriage named in the syllabus described neutrally, practices now outlawed (child and forced marriage) stated as illegal, and the value of marriage (dignity, respect, cooperation, continuity of the family). Types of marriage are her.identity.marriage-types.

concepts.name: Men and women in marriage
concepts.description: Form 4. Roles and responsibilities of men and women in marriage in indigenous and contemporary families, how and why roles are changing (education, employment, law, urbanisation), shared responsibilities, and equality of spouses under the Constitution. Gender equality in society generally is her.rights.gender-equality.

concepts.name: Birth and death rites and ceremonies
concepts.description: Forms 2 and 3. Indigenous birth rites and ceremonies (care of mother and baby, naming, protecting the child) and death rites and ceremonies (announcing a death, burial customs, mourning, cleansing, the later bringing-home ceremony), how they differ between groups and religions, their significance and the threats they face. Community gatherings in general are her.identity.community-gatherings.

concepts.name: Indigenous forms of entertainment
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Indigenous entertainment: folklore and storytelling, games (e.g. nhodo, tsoro/isafuba, mahumbwe in outline), dance and song, music instruments (mbira, drums, hosho), and the other uses of entertainment (education, socialisation, passing on values, exercise, identity). Contemporary dance, drama, sport and the arts are her.culture.arts-sport.

concepts.name: Dance, drama, sport, arts and culture
concepts.description: Forms 3 and 4. Dance and drama as forms of entertainment, leisure and employment (traditional dances such as Jerusarema/Mbende, Isitshikitsha, Muchongoyo in outline), and the importance of sport, arts and culture (entertainment, socialisation, identity, unity, employment creation, tourism, national pride). Creative skills as enterprise are her.production.enterprise-skills.

concepts.name: Hunter-gatherer and herder communities: the San and the Khoikhoi
concepts.description: Form 1. The San (hunter-gatherers) and Khoikhoi (herders): way of life, social, political and economic organisation, rock paintings in Zimbabwe (e.g. in the Matobo Hills), and the heritage they passed on (hunting skills and tools, tool making, rock art, knowledge of plants and medicines, tanning). No dates beyond approximate ranges; respectful, no stereotypes.

concepts.name: Indigenous political structures and chieftainship
concepts.description: Form 1. The hierarchy of indigenous leadership (king or paramount chief, chief (ishe/induna), headman (sadunhu), village head (sabhuku)), the roles of each, how chiefs are chosen and installed (succession, spirit mediums, regalia), the significance of chieftainship, and traditional leaders today in outline (Chapter 15 of the Constitution).

concepts.name: Early Iron Age societies
concepts.description: Form 2. Early Iron Age farming communities in Zimbabwe (e.g. Gokomere/Ziwa traditions; dates only as approximate ranges, first millennium CE), their tools, iron smelting, pottery, crops and livestock, villages, and their social, economic and political activities. Late Iron Age states are separate concepts.

concepts.name: Late Iron Age states: Great Zimbabwe and Mutapa
concepts.description: Form 2. Great Zimbabwe (rise, stone buildings, cattle, gold and ivory trade with the coast, religion, political, social and economic organisation, decline presented as theories; built by the ancestors of the Shona) and the Mutapa state (origins in tradition, organisation, trade, tribute, mhondoro spirit mediums, contact with the Portuguese in outline, decline). Heritage-level depth; World Heritage status is her.heritage.world-heritage-sites.

concepts.name: Late Iron Age states: Torwa, Rozvi and Ndebele
concepts.description: Form 2. The Torwa state and Khami in outline, the Rozvi state under Changamire Dombo (rise, organisation, decline), and the Ndebele state (Mzilikazi's settlement in the late 1830s, political, social and economic organisation, Lobengula in outline). Heritage-level depth; the fall of the Ndebele state is her.colonisation.anglo-ndebele-war.

concepts.name: Contributions of Iron Age communities to contemporary societies
concepts.description: Form 2. What Iron Age societies passed on: farming and crops, iron working and crafts, mining, trade, stone building, political structures and traditional leadership, traditional medicine, religious beliefs, and how these contributions remain significant in contemporary Zimbabwe.

concepts.name: Missionaries, explorers, traders, concession seekers, adventurers and hunters
concepts.description: Form 2. The groups of foreigners who came to Zimbabwe in the nineteenth century (missionaries such as the London Missionary Society at Inyati from 1859, explorers such as David Livingstone, traders, hunters, concession seekers and adventurers), their activities, and the role each played in preparing for colonisation. The treaties and occupation are her.colonisation.colonisation.

concepts.name: Colonisation: the Berlin Conference, treaties and occupation
concepts.description: Form 3. Causes of colonisation (economic, political, strategic, social), the Berlin Conference (1884-85) and its resolutions in outline, the treaties leading to the colonisation of Zimbabwe (Grobler Treaty 1887, Moffat Treaty 1888, Rudd Concession 30 October 1888), the Royal Charter (1889) and the British South Africa Company, the Pioneer Column and occupation (Fort Salisbury, 12 September 1890), and African responses.

concepts.name: The Anglo-Ndebele War, 1893-94
concepts.description: Form 3. Causes (Company ambitions for land and gold, the Victoria incident, border disputes), the course of the war (battles of Shangani and Bembesi, the fall of Bulawayo, Lobengula's flight and death, the Shangani Patrol) in outline, and its effects on the Ndebele (loss of land and cattle, reserves, forced labour) and on the Company.

concepts.name: The First Chimurenga/Umvukela, 1896-97
concepts.description: Form 3. Causes (loss of land and cattle, forced labour, hut tax, brutality of Company police, natural disasters such as rinderpest, drought and locusts, the Jameson Raid), the course of the risings in Matabeleland (from March 1896) and Mashonaland (from June 1896), the role of spirit mediums, reasons for defeat and the results. Coordination between the risings presented as a debate. The heroes and heroines and how they are remembered are her.colonisation.first-chimurenga-heroes.

concepts.name: Heroes and heroines of the First Chimurenga/Umvukela
concepts.description: Form 3. Leaders of the First Chimurenga/Umvukela and their roles: spirit mediums Mbuya Nehanda (Charwe Nyakasikana) and Sekuru Kaguvi (Gumboreshumba), both executed in April 1898; Mkwati; chiefs such as Mashayamombe and Makoni; Ndebele leaders in outline; why they are honoured today (statues, names, songs) and the significance of remembering them. Only well-established names and facts.

concepts.name: Expropriation of land and resources in colonial Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 3 (Topics 4 and 5). How colonial rule took land, cattle, minerals and labour: land alienation and reserves, the Land Apportionment Act (1930), the Native Land Husbandry Act (1951) and the Land Tenure Act (1969), taxes and forced labour, ownership of mines, forests and wildlife by settlers and companies, and the effects on indigenous people. Land redistribution after 1980 is her.production.land-ownership.

concepts.name: The Second Chimurenga/Umvukela (liberation struggle), 1966-79
concepts.description: Form 3. Causes of the liberation struggle (land, political exclusion, discrimination, UDI and failed talks), its course in outline (Chinhoyi, 28 April 1966; the shift to guerrilla warfare in the 1970s; ZANLA and ZIPRA, both treated fairly; bases in Mozambique and Zambia), attempts at settlement, the Lancaster House Agreement (signed 21 December 1979), and the results (independence on 18 April 1980, costs of the war). The roles of the people and the heroes are her.liberation.roles-heroes.

concepts.name: The roles of the people in the liberation struggle; national heroes and heroines
concepts.description: Form 3. Roles played in the liberation struggle by the masses (peasants who fed and hid fighters), freedom fighters, mujibhas and chimbwidos (zvimbwido), spirit mediums, chiefs, churches, workers and students, refugees, the Frontline States and other supporters; national heroes and heroines: what the status means and how heroes are honoured (National Heroes Acre, provincial heroes acres) in neutral terms. Liberation heritage sites are her.heritage.liberation-sites.

concepts.name: Independent Zimbabwe: the gains of independence
concepts.description: Form 4. Independence on 18 April 1980, the policy of reconciliation, social gains (expansion of education and health services, rights for women such as the Legal Age of Majority Act 1982), economic gains in outline, land redistribution (pointer to her.production.land-ownership), and national unity: the Unity Accord of 22 December 1987. Facts well established; no statistics unless documented.

concepts.name: Challenges faced by Zimbabwe since independence
concepts.description: Form 4. Challenges faced by the government after 1980: droughts and natural disasters (e.g. Cyclone Idai, March 2019), economic difficulties (structural adjustment from 1991, hyperinflation in the late 2000s, currency changes in outline), sanctions or restrictive measures from the early 2000s with the different views on them, disease (HIV/AIDS), brain drain, and the disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands in the 1980s (Gukurahundi) acknowledged factually and sensitively. Balanced, no blame of living politicians.

concepts.name: Systems of governance: democracy and autocracy
concepts.description: Form 4. Meaning of governance and government; systems of governance (democracy (direct and representative), autocracy, dictatorship, monarchy, and indigenous systems in outline), characteristics of democracy (free elections, rule of law, separation of powers, rights, accountability) and autocracy, with a comparison. No labelling of present-day countries.

concepts.name: Structures and functions of central government
concepts.description: Form 4. The three arms of government under the 2013 Constitution: the Executive (President, Vice-Presidents, Cabinet), the Legislature (Parliament: Senate and National Assembly; law-making, oversight, representation) and the Judiciary (courts, independence), their functions, separation of powers and checks and balances, and the importance of government. The court hierarchy is her.constitution.laws-courts.

concepts.name: Local government structures
concepts.description: Form 4. The tiers of government (national, provincial and metropolitan, local) and devolution (Chapter 14 of the Constitution) in outline; local authorities (urban councils and rural district councils), councillors, mayors and council officials, their functions (water, refuse, roads, clinics, by-laws, rates), sources of income, how citizens participate, and the role of traditional leaders in local governance.

concepts.name: Government as a social service provider
concepts.description: Form 4. Social services provided by government (education, health, housing and shelter, water and sanitation, social welfare for vulnerable people such as fee assistance and care for orphans, transport and electricity in outline), why government provides them, how they are funded (taxes), the challenges in providing them, and the role of citizens and partners.

concepts.name: Zimbabwe in regional and continental organisations
concepts.description: Form 4. Zimbabwe's membership of SADC (from SADCC 1980; SADC 1992), COMESA and the African Union (OAU 25 May 1963; AU 2002): aims, structure in outline, benefits to Zimbabwe and obligations, and the challenges these organisations face. The UN and NAM are her.governance.international-organisations.

concepts.name: Zimbabwe in international organisations
concepts.description: Form 4. Zimbabwe's membership of the United Nations (founded 24 October 1945; Zimbabwe a member since 1980) and its main organs and agencies relevant to Zimbabwe (UNICEF, UNESCO, WHO, WFP), and the Non-Aligned Movement (founded 1961; Harare summit 1986): aims, benefits to Zimbabwe and obligations. The Commonwealth in neutral outline only (withdrawal in 2003); no claims about its current status.

concepts.name: National symbols
concepts.description: Form 1. Meaning of national symbols and heritage; the national flag (colours, the white triangle, the red star and the Zimbabwe Bird, and the meanings commonly taught), the coat of arms, the national anthem (not quoted), the Zimbabwe Bird, the public seal (section 4 of the Constitution), and the significance of national symbols (identity, unity, patriotism, respect and correct use). The pledge is her.heritage.schools-pledge.

concepts.name: National monuments and shrines
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. Meaning of national monuments and shrines; examples (monuments such as Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Naletale, Chinhoyi Caves, Domboshava; shrines such as the National Heroes Acre, provincial heroes acres, Njelele), their significance (history, identity, religion, tourism, education), the role of National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe, and how they are protected. World Heritage listing is her.heritage.world-heritage-sites.

concepts.name: World heritage sites in Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Forms 3 and 4. Meaning of a World Heritage Site and the role of UNESCO; Zimbabwe's five sites: Mana Pools National Park, Sapi and Chewore Safari Areas (1984), Great Zimbabwe National Monument (1986), Khami Ruins National Monument (1986), Mosi-oa-Tunya/Victoria Falls (1989, shared with Zambia) and Matobo Hills (2003); why each was listed, the benefits (tourism, conservation, pride) and the threats they face.

concepts.name: Liberation war heritage sites
concepts.description: Form 4. Liberation war heritage sites in neighbouring countries (Chimoio and Nyadzonia in Mozambique, Freedom Camp in Zambia, and others), what happened there stated factually and respectfully with dates (Nyadzonia, August 1976; Chimoio, November 1977; Freedom Camp, October 1978) and casualty numbers only as approximate estimates, the importance of preserving and visiting such sites, and regional cooperation in preserving them.

concepts.name: National events and celebrations
concepts.description: Form 2. National events and their dates (Independence Day 18 April; Heroes Day and Defence Forces Day in August; Unity Day 22 December; Africa Day 25 May; national tree-planting day in December), what each commemorates, how they are celebrated, and the significance of participating in and commemorating national events (unity, remembrance, patriotism).

concepts.name: The National Schools Pledge
concepts.description: Forms 1 to 4. The National Schools Pledge (introduced in schools in 2016): its main ideas in paraphrase (respect for God, the flag, the heroes, the nation and its resources, honesty, dignity and hard work), its relation to the national flag and anthem, and its significance; the public debate when it was introduced mentioned neutrally. The full text is not reproduced.

concepts.name: Natural resources as national heritage
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Meaning of natural resources, renewable and non-renewable resources, Zimbabwe's natural resources (land, minerals, animals, birds, plants and forests, rivers and water), their importance (food, income, employment, tourism, culture) and why they are heritage held for future generations. Ownership and access are her.heritage.resource-ownership; conservation is her.production.resource-conservation.

concepts.name: Ownership of and access to natural resources
concepts.description: Forms 3 and 4. Key natural resources in national development, ownership of natural resources during the colonial era in outline (detail in her.colonisation.expropriation), government efforts since 1980 to improve indigenous people's access to minerals, wildlife, forests and water (indigenisation and economic empowerment, community-based schemes such as CAMPFIRE, constitutional provisions), and the effectiveness of these efforts with recognised benefits and problems. Land redistribution is her.production.land-ownership.

concepts.name: The constitution-making process
concepts.description: Form 1. Meaning of a constitution, why countries need one, why Zimbabwe needed a new constitution, and the making of the 2013 Constitution (the parliamentary select committee COPAC from 2009, public outreach, drafting, the referendum of 16 March 2013, signing into law on 22 May 2013), and the role of citizens in constitution-making. The Lancaster House constitution and earlier attempts (the rejected 2000 draft) are her.constitution.lancaster-to-2013.

concepts.name: Contents and key features of the Constitution of Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. The structure of the 2013 Constitution (18 chapters), founding values and principles, national objectives, key features (supremacy of the Constitution, the Declaration of Rights, tiers of government, the 16 official languages, rights to education and health care, independent commissions, land, traditional leaders) and their significance, and the importance of the Constitution. Rights in detail are her.constitution.declaration-of-rights.

concepts.name: The Declaration of Rights
concepts.description: Form 2. Chapter 4 of the Constitution: meaning of fundamental human rights and freedoms, examples (life, personal liberty, equality and non-discrimination, education, health care, freedom of expression, assembly and conscience, property, fair trial, a clean environment), rights of specific groups in outline, limitation of rights, enforcement through the courts and the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission, and the duties that come with rights. Children's and vulnerable groups' rights are her.rights.*.

concepts.name: Zimbabwean citizenship
concepts.description: Form 2. Meaning of citizenship and a citizen, the ways of becoming a Zimbabwean citizen (by birth, by descent, by registration), the rights, privileges and duties of citizens, identity documents as proof, and loss of citizenship in outline only if certain. Civic responsibilities are her.rights.civic-responsibilities.

concepts.name: Rules, laws and the courts of Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 2. Rules and laws and the difference between them, sources and types of law (the Constitution, Acts of Parliament, statutory instruments and by-laws, customary law, common law), the courts of Zimbabwe and their hierarchy and jurisdiction (Constitutional Court, Supreme Court, High Court, Labour Court, Administrative Court, magistrates courts, customary law (local) courts), and the importance of the rule of law.

concepts.name: The electoral system of Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 3. Meaning of elections and an electoral system, the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission, voter registration and the right to vote at 18, harmonised elections every five years, the election of the President (more than half of the votes, or a run-off), constituency and proportional-representation seats in Parliament in outline, by-elections and referendums, and the features of free and fair elections. Party politics and results of particular elections are out.

concepts.name: From the Lancaster House constitution to a home-grown constitution
concepts.description: Form 4. Key provisions of the Lancaster House constitution (1979) (reserved seats for whites for seven years, protected property and land clauses, the Declaration of Rights, amendments made later such as the executive presidency), why a new constitution was needed (its foreign drafting, the many amendments, demands for reform), earlier attempts (the draft rejected in the February 2000 referendum), and the importance of a home-grown constitution. The 2013 process itself is her.constitution.making.

concepts.name: Entitlements of men and women in indigenous society
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 4. Indigenous entitlements of women (the mother's cow (mombe yeumai/inkomo yohlanga), the mother's piece of land (tseu), the kitchen, a share in bride wealth) and of men (authority, land, tools, protection and identity of the family), the importance of these entitlements, and how they compare with contemporary rights.

concepts.name: Children's rights and responsibilities
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Children's rights (section 81 of the Constitution; the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child in outline) at home (shelter, education, security, care) and at school (education, safety, information, being heard), children's responsibilities and duties at home and at school, and the difference between rights and responsibilities. Child labour is her.global.child-labour.

concepts.name: Rights and responsibilities of vulnerable groups
concepts.description: Form 3. Rights and responsibilities of the elderly, persons with disabilities, women, war veterans and other vulnerable groups (children, orphans) under the Constitution (sections 80 to 84 in outline), the challenges these groups face, and how government, communities and individuals support them.

concepts.name: Roles and civic responsibilities of citizens
concepts.description: Forms 2 and 3. The roles and responsibilities of Zimbabwean citizens (defending the country's sovereignty, upholding national values and the Constitution, obeying the law, paying taxes, voting, protecting heritage and the environment), and civic responsibilities at community and national level (security, education, health, shelter, community projects), with the importance of active citizenship. Volunteering is her.rights.voluntary-activities.

concepts.name: Voluntary community activities
concepts.description: Forms 2 and 4. Meaning of voluntary community activities, examples (clean-ups, helping the elderly and the sick, tree planting, community gardens, school projects), community needs that require voluntary intervention and the differences between rural and urban needs, and the importance of volunteering for the community and the volunteer.

concepts.name: Gender equity and equality in contemporary Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 4. Meaning of gender, sex, gender roles, gender equity and gender equality, gender stereotypes and discrimination, constitutional provisions (gender balance and equality between men and women; the Zimbabwe Gender Commission), international conventions (CEDAW, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the Maputo Protocol) in outline, and progress and barriers. Gender-based violence is her.rights.gender-based-violence.

concepts.name: Gender-based violence and gender advocacy
concepts.description: Form 4. Types of gender-based violence (physical, sexual, emotional, economic), causes and effects, the Domestic Violence Act (2007) and where victims get help, pressure groups and advocates for gender equality (e.g. Msasa Project, Padare/Enkundleni Men's Forum on Gender), and the strengths and weaknesses of advocacy. No graphic detail.

concepts.name: Factors of production and access to them
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 4. The factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship), their rewards in outline, their significance, access to factors of production in Zimbabwe and government efforts to help people access them (land, loans and funds for small enterprises, training). Factors that hold production back are her.production.inhibiting-factors.

concepts.name: Industry: indigenous and contemporary, and types of industry
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Meaning of industry, indigenous industries (iron smelting, pottery, weaving, basketry, mining) and contemporary industries in Zimbabwe, the types of industry (primary, secondary, tertiary), economic activities in each, and their importance. Manufacturing methods are her.production.manufacturing.

concepts.name: The informal sector
concepts.description: Forms 1, 2 and 3. Meaning and characteristics of the informal sector, examples in Zimbabwe (vending, cross-border trading, small-scale manufacturing and repairs), the difference between the formal and informal sectors, the importance of the informal sector, the constraints it faces (capital, skills, insurance, premises, regulation) and possible solutions.

concepts.name: Storage and preservation of indigenous and contemporary foods
concepts.description: Form 1. Indigenous foods (e.g. madora/amacimbi, mufushwa/umfushwa, dovi/idobi, small grains) and contemporary foods, indigenous storage and preservation methods (sun-drying, smoking, salting, granaries (dura/ingqolobane), storing in pots and pits) and contemporary methods (canning, refrigeration, freezing, packaging), and the importance of indigenous and contemporary foods (nutrition, food security, heritage). Hygiene stated correctly.

concepts.name: Indigenous conservation and management of resources
concepts.description: Form 2. Indigenous methods of conserving and managing natural resources (taboos, totems, sacred places and forests, rules of chiefs and indigenous laws, seasonal restrictions, indigenous knowledge systems (IKS)), how they worked, and an assessment of their effectiveness then and today. Contemporary institutions and laws are her.production.resource-conservation.

concepts.name: Contemporary methods of manufacturing goods
concepts.description: Form 2. Meaning of manufacturing, the processes of manufacturing (processing, assembling, packaging) and production methods (handicraft and mechanised, mass production) in outline, examples from Zimbabwe, and the advantages and disadvantages of modern methods.

concepts.name: National strategic reserves
concepts.description: Form 3. Meaning of national strategic reserves, examples (strategic grain reserves held by the Grain Marketing Board; fuel reserves, formerly through NOCZIM), their functions (food and fuel security, price stability, emergencies) and their significance, and the challenges of keeping reserves. Company details only if certain.

concepts.name: Land ownership in Zimbabwe
concepts.description: Form 3 (Topic 8) with Form 4 (Topic 5) land reform. Types of land tenure (communal, freehold, leasehold, state land, resettlement land), the legacy of colonial land laws in outline (detail in her.colonisation.expropriation), the measures taken to redistribute land since 1980 (willing-buyer willing-seller in the 1980s and 1990s, the fast-track land reform programme from 2000, Chapter 16 of the Constitution), and aims, recognised benefits and recognised problems presented in a balanced way.

concepts.name: Factors inhibiting production and their solutions
concepts.description: Form 4. Factors that inhibit production in Zimbabwe (restrictive legislation, lack of capital, sanctions or restrictive measures with the different views, skills shortages and brain drain, outdated technology, power and water shortages, drought), their effects, and possible solutions (capacity building, technology, investment, skills training, policy).

concepts.name: Enterprise skills and employment creation
concepts.description: Form 4. Meaning of enterprise and enterprise skills (creativity, risk-taking, planning, financial literacy, marketing), self-reliance projects and creative industries that create employment (music, art, sport, dance, pottery, poetry, theatre, film, basketry, weaving), and how enterprise skills contribute to the growth of the economy.

concepts.name: Conservation and preservation of resources
concepts.description: Form 4. Contemporary methods of conserving and preserving natural and cultural resources, the institutions involved (Environmental Management Agency under the Environmental Management Act, Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority, Forestry Commission, National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe), laws and their enforcement, and a comparison with indigenous methods (detail in her.production.indigenous-conservation).

concepts.name: Environmental issues and the preservation of natural resources
concepts.description: Form 1. Environmental issues facing Zimbabwe and the world in outline (deforestation, poaching, overuse of water, loss of wildlife and biodiversity), the forms of natural resources affected (land, minerals, forests, rivers, dams) and strategies that individuals, schools and communities use to preserve them. Pollution, land degradation and climate change are separate concepts.

concepts.name: Pollution
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. Meaning and types of pollution (air, water, land, noise), sources and levels of pollution, effects on people, animals and the environment, and ways of reducing pollution, with an assessment of mitigation measures (laws, EMA, recycling, cleaner technology, awareness). Waste management systems are her.global.waste-management.

concepts.name: Land degradation
concepts.description: Form 3. Meaning, causes (deforestation, overgrazing, poor farming methods, veld fires, illegal gold panning, urban expansion), effects (soil erosion, siltation of rivers and dams, loss of fertility, desertification) and measures to reduce land degradation (afforestation, contour ridges, rotational grazing, laws).

concepts.name: Hazards, risks and disasters; disaster management
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 2. Meaning of hazard, risk and disaster; types (environmental/natural, biological, mechanical/man-made); causes and effects of droughts and floods; the impact of disasters on people and the environment; and disaster mitigation and management (preparedness, early warning, Civil Protection, relief, recovery), with Zimbabwean examples such as Cyclone Idai (2019). Climate change is her.global.climate-change.

concepts.name: Climate change
concepts.description: Form 2. Meaning of climate change and the difference from weather, causes (greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture), effects on Zimbabwe and the world (droughts, floods, heat, crop failure, health), and adaptation (drought-tolerant crops, water harvesting, conservation farming) and mitigation measures (renewable energy, afforestation).

concepts.name: Pandemics and infectious diseases
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. Meaning of endemic, epidemic and pandemic; infectious diseases named in the syllabus (HIV/AIDS, Ebola, cholera, dysentery) and COVID-19, their causes and spread in outline, social, economic and political impacts, and prevention and mitigation measures (hygiene, safe water, testing and treatment, vaccination, public health measures), with an evaluation. Accurate, non-stigmatising health information only.

concepts.name: Chronic illnesses
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. Meaning of chronic (non-communicable) illness; diabetes and hypertension (and others in outline): risk factors, effects on individuals, families and the nation, prevention (diet, exercise, avoiding tobacco and alcohol abuse, screening) and management. General health information only, no medical advice beyond seeing a health worker.

concepts.name: Human trafficking
concepts.description: Forms 1 and 3. Meaning of human trafficking and the difference from smuggling, forms (forced labour, sexual exploitation, domestic servitude, child trafficking, organ removal), causes (poverty, unemployment, false job offers, conflict), effects on victims and society, and prevention and mitigation measures (awareness, laws, reporting, safe migration). No graphic detail.

concepts.name: Waste management
concepts.description: Form 4. Types of waste (domestic, industrial, agricultural, medical, electronic), the problems of poor waste disposal, waste management strategies and approaches (reduce, reuse, recycle; collection, landfills, composting, incineration), the roles of local authorities, EMA and citizens, and an evaluation of the approaches.

concepts.name: Child labour
concepts.description: Form 4. Meaning and forms of child labour, its causes and effects, laws and conventions against it (the Constitution, the Children's Act and Labour Act in outline, ILO conventions, the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child), and the difference between child labour and children's responsibilities (age-appropriate chores that do not harm health or schooling).
